decision.audit_notes: Verified current-session dialogue; decision evidence remapped to cleaned source.

evidence.text: Okay, by saying this. I'm going to give you 100,000 at 15.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Hi. I'm Laura from Teamable, and we've built the best way to hire the right teammates via data driven referrals.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: The average person has between 500 and 1500 connections across Facebook, LinkedIn, the oldest social network which is their email. The thing is, they don't know necessarily who those people are and they're not thinking about them in terms of positions at their companies.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: So we did what any normal person would do, we quit our nice lives and we moved out here to a garage at Palo Alto. And so we're raising $1 million to accelerate our growth.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Is this your first company?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yes. Yeah. But I was an investment banker, you know, so I was in a lot of these meetings with other people's companies.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Tell us more about how it works.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Well, I'll just use an example of a company we're launching in a few days, is Medallia, which is pre-IPO.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: And it's very, very effective.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So you're replacing recruiters?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yes, we are replacing agencies. We were just talking to Warby Parker in New York yesterday - their engineers are getting between 20 and 100 messages a day. They're ignoring them. But when it comes from their friend that they used to work at Google with they respond.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So the employee is empowered to reach out to their friends once there's a match?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah. That's the biggest hold point.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Hey, we all know referrals make great hires, we all don't have time to go through our networks every time a new position opens. Can you take 30 seconds and upload your contacts into Teamable. By the way, you're just giving the names, no one can see your Facebook wall, no one can see your LinkedIn. It's like a spreadsheet type thing.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: I think it makes sense. Like, I never respond to recruiters.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: I'm sure most of you haven't applied to a job since you were in college, like me.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Any good person doesn't apply for a job, right?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: That's not true.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: I've never hired anybody who was looking for a job. I've hired people who are great people. Great people aren't just available.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: So there's a huge, the biggest challenge my companies all have is talent right now. So I feel the need. There are other players in this space, broadly. Jobvite.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: LinkedIn.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Doing all sorts of other stuff. I'm still struggling for what you do that's differentiated.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah, so a couple things we do that's differentiated is we tap into social graphs. Like GitHub and Facebook, which LinkedIn, for example, can't do. So we've spent a lot of time in stealth building that capability. It's not easy. The other way that we're different is a lot of companies have tried to automate the matches, But the problem is if you automate the matches, one bad match and people start hating the software. Right? Whereas if you let the recruiters drive it and pick out the matches, then the matches are 100% correct.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: How's it going over all, for you? As a first-time entrepreneur?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: I mean, I went through the darkness last year where it was like hell.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: You were in the trough of sorrow?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: And people were like no one is going to pay you to use their own contacts. That kind of stuff. And I really didn't know... Everything I did I didn't know what I was doing. But Silicon Valley has been really great and so things have been -- it's good now.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: So tell me about...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Revenue.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: We've been growing at 47% month over month. We're at 42 MRR now.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: We closed last quarter with two sales, we will have closed $225k in new bookings. We're good.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Take it from the beginning.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: From the beginning? So we're at 42,000 monthly recurring revenue.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: No. Take us, back up, back up.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Okay. We charge on a subscription basis. And we charge per employee per month.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: How much do you charge?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah, we charge sometimes as much as $20 per employee per month.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What's the average, though?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: I actually don't know the average. But it's very close to that $20. We've done some bigger deals now that are like a thousand people, and that will go down to like $8 per employee per month.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: But that's sort of weird, because per employee... Shouldn't it be based on how many people they're hiring?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: No, it's per employee per month, because every employee comes with a value, which is the candidates in their network and their ability to influence their network. And then also like, we can't account for their close rates.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: So this can scale infinitely? You could scale up to hundreds of thousands of employees?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah. We can do anyone.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Customers pay us up front.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: They pay you all up front?

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: It's good for cash flow perspective.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: A lot of times. Because they're budget conscious, so we use that as part of the negotiation. Okay, great, you pay us up front, you can do $15 per employee per month.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Makes sense.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I think you're disciplined. I think that's actually the best way to grow. What's your burn?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: What's our burn? It's, $20k.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How many people?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: We have 27.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: I made a contrarian bet on Armenia. I'm ethnically Armenian. So I went there and they have a lot of those top engineers like those other Eastern European countries, but no one is tapping into it. And so we're the best game in Armenia. We have great engineers.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: What do you pay them?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: I'm not saying on the... They're the cheapest for the region, so-. And I'm blaming my co-founders on this. They're Armenian, so they set the prices.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I love the fact that you're doing that. I love it. That must give you amazing pride.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: It does. That's how I made it through the darkness. If we're talking about like, honestly, if it weren't for creating an opportunity for Armenia through those periods where things didn't work and where no one wanted to buy it and all that stuff. I would have just given up. But it was really for that, that kept me through. And it's created immense pride and hope and things like that over there.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Now we won't take anything less than a $15 million cap.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: How much are you raising?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: We would take another 150.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So you're taking a 150 at a 15?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: What's your MRR going to be by the end of this year, do you think?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: By the end of this year, we'll get to that 100k.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So 15 is a little bit hefty valuation for...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I agree.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Because you're not yet at the Series A.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: It's a cap, right. So it's your chance to get in or just not.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: But why are you raising 150k?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: If you don't need it?

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yeah, I don't get that.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: You don't need it.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: You don't need us.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Because there's 40,000 listeners. All of which hiring is a pain point for.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I like your strategic mind.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Very opportunistic.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Appreciate your honesty.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: So does anyone want to get in at the…

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I think the valuation that you're offering us is a little rich at this stage. I know that you have better insight into where you'll be in a few months than we do, of course. But I'm very interested. I'm just a little turned off by a $15 million valuation at $42,000 MRR.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: But 47% month over month growth.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Yeah, but you're asking us to invest at valuation levels three months from now.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: And enterprise deals. Like, people would invest in that if you had just one six figure deal. Like how many companies have six figure enterprise deals? Not that many?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: But I can tell you, companies that we invest in at $42,000 MRR, which is where you are today, they're not getting anywhere near $15 million valuation. I know for you, you're in a good position, because you don't need the money.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: They also don't have the same cash flow profile that we have. Because think about the unit economics plus the cost of engineering is a fraction. So our total engineering costs is $15,000 including office a month. So with the cash that we will throw off...

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: That's all part of we’re cash flow positive, which other companies...

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: No, that's part of also the growth, the cash flow.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Look, I look at a ton of SAAS businesses. There are other businesses that take cash up front and are cash flow positive. There are tons of them. And I've got a company in my portfolio that's doing a few hundred K MRR but actually they're taking million dollar contracts up front. So it's not unique.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Are they valued at less than 15 million?

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: No. But they're doing 8x the business you are and they're valued at 25 or 30 million. So it's a different level.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: I want to be in. Right? I want to invest. I'm just having trouble with the number. So, I think, regrettably I'm going to have to pass at 15 million.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Is there a number at which you wouldn't pass?

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Yeah. I think for me at 10 I would do it.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: No. Can't do it.

turns.speaker: Jake
turns.text: So for me, I think there's three things. First, I think I'm probably not a great investor for you, because I don't really know the hiring, referral, talent space very well. So for me, I don't think I could add a ton of value to your company. Two, like everyone's saying, I think the valuation is definitely a little high. Maybe it makes sense, from what you're seeing you know you can close in two months, But today I've got to value you at 42,000 MRR and that's more like a $4 or 5 million cap. 10 million is fairly generous. 15 is really off the charts at that. The last one which is I think the elephant in the room is, there was a 30 second moment of brutal honesty in your pitch. And I found that a big personal turn off. So, if you're here because you want the publicity, and you're open to raising money, that's fine. Even though you're not here really to raise money. But the way it was delivered felt very much like this is just a promotional opportunity for me and I don't care about any of you here or what value you can add. And so for that, I think that was just a little flub, I think you're a very nice person, but it was definitely a personal turnoff. And in first impressions, that can kill a deal, at least for me.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I have a totally different view. I get pitched 60 to 70 companies a month. And I hear the same standard banal platitude rhetoric. Like, it was refreshing to hear that. And I think you're scrappy, and I think you're opportunistic, and I think you have grit and like gumption, and I think that's fucking awesome. That's rare. I don't see that in the valley that much.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: Howie, let me ask you a question though. Based on what you've seen — we're going to talk about you in front of you —

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Fine.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: — do you see her as a founder who is teachable?

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: You know, I don't see it... It's interesting, because I sort of pride myself on being a... I started my fund because I think I can identify talent and I think I can read people really well. And that's when at the early stage I'm mostly betting on people. And as brutally honest as you are, and maybe just because I have a lot of experience, I love working with East Coast founders and companies, it's just like it's not an ego or hubris thing. I actually do think you'd be open if we worked together to taking feedback. You don't seem cantankerous. You actually just seem like you're crushing it, to be honest. That's what I get. And I personally, I do think it's over-valued, but I do think that this could be one of those opportunities where it's like a half a billion to a billion dollar exit, if not more, based on your hustle, based on all the things you've said, based on your traction, based on you overcoming existential risk and digging yourself out of the trough of sorrow, and then actually delivering results. You're actually walking the walk. Like, I'm in. I probably want to go in for 25 or 30 or something like that. And I'm a creative, and I have empathy for you, and I'm an operator myself. So this gap between venture and entrepreneur is actually very small for me. So I like getting my hands dirty. I like working very closely with my founders.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Let me understand this, Howie.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Yes, Jillian.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So, what I heard from Laura is, "I'm standing firm at 15". This is what I heard.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay. but everybody who has spoken so far has said, "I would come in, but I would come in at a little bit lower". But if you're going to give Howie a lower valuation because he's going to tell you how valuable he is, then you should give that opportunity to all of us, don't you think? Or to the ones that you feel will add as much as he will.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: we're going to map it out with real numbers and stuff. It's not just, oh hey, the standard pitch that VCs say.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I can actually, I'll be very honest, and I'm not going to be humble on this, because pretty much everybody who is listening will know this.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Don't be humble, that's like a woman thing, anyway. I'm trying not to...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I'm not a humble person. I can pick up the phone and pretty much call at the highest level, the CEOs, at least to...

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Of which industry?

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Pretty much any industry. So I'm old. Let me start there.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: I didn't say it.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I've been around a long time. But let me just speak about you. You're a heat-seeking missile. Absolutely. I love your grit. And I love your edge.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Thanks.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I was offended, I got to admit, about what you said.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Sorry.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: But this is what I tell founders all the time. You can be tenacious, but stay gracious. Okay. That's really, really important. Because business is about relationships. Bottom line. So just be a little bit careful. You want to be cocky, you're okay, that's all okay. And you want to get marketing from this. Good for you. I mean, yes, absolutely. And I applaud you on that. It was the presentation of the reality of it. It was like, I don't need you.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: And it's actually not the reality. Because one of the reasons is that I want to make sure our cap table is filled with female minority founders. And the fact that you were on here is actually one of the main reasons that I wanted to come. Because, really.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Oh.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: And totally redeems herself.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So, I really love this. I love you. I love the fact that you're finding jobs for females in tech. I love that piece. Every inch of me wants to put 100 grand into this. I'm absolutely choking on the 15 million. And I'm wondering if there's any possible way, that you would come down...

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: The three of us should get some tequila.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Some tequila would be good.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I've got a great tequila company. You get tequila for life with $100 grand.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: No, I don't need that. You don't want to give me that.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: There goes the company!

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Shots for everyone!

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: So I guess the question is back at you. When we said to you 15, you definitely posted it back to us and said, what would you feel comfortable with? Or what would be good? So I'm slinging it back on to you. What do you think? Do you think you could open this up for a couple of us who are interested or whatever at 13? Would you, I mean we're talking about splicing hairs here.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah. I'm thinking about the whole chessboard. Not just what's in this room.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: And it's not the money. It's not just the money.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: At the end of the day it's actually not going to matter in terms of whether it's 10, 11, 12 or 15. It's actually not going to matter.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: At ten? Ten's like no. Ten definitely no.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: We could fill out that whole 150k at ten.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: I really came in with a real price that I was like...

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: 12? Come on. Give us 12.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: I actually really do want to talk about the real things where you would add value. Because we've been having a lot of these conversations for real. And so I do want to...

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: We should all talk. I'd love to chip in as well.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: I'm going to end this.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: All right, let's end it. I gotta go. Let's go.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Okay, by saying this. I'm going to give you 100,000 at 15.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Wow.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Hold on. There's a caveat here. If after sitting down with me and having a larger conversation, okay, you feel that I add more value than you expected me to, then you will consider lowering the valuation.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Sounds good.

turns.speaker: Jillian
turns.text: Deal. All right. That's it.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yay! I got another female investor! Woo! Thank you. Welcome to the team. And we'll talk.

turns.speaker: Howie
turns.text: Yeah and I'm in for $25k.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: I would say I'm in for $50 at 15m with a 35% discount.
